title: US Outposts Were Dangerous Bubbles: How the War on Terror Trapped Itself
dek: US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became magnets for conflict. The harder they fought, the heavier they got, losing mobility until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.
why: Wesley Morgan served in Afghanistan himself and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the War on Terror: tactical success coexisting with strategic failure. Worth the time of anyone thinking about war and organizations.
who: Readers interested in war history, US military tactics and organizational behavior, especially those curious about the inside story of the War on Terror and how military decisions get made.
skip: The last 5 minutes of football chat can be skipped.

points.body: In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan embedded with troops entering the Pech Valley in Afghanistan and found that US outposts meant to provide security for villages had in fact become ‘dangerous bubbles’ that drew conflict toward the villagers. American and enemy casualties were both low; the people who truly suffered were in the villages outside the wire. That contrast drove him to ask who built these outposts, why, and when — questions that eventually became his book The Hardest Place.

points.h: The US military grew heavier and dumber
points.body: From 2006 to 2010, US forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, tethered to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006 the 10th Mountain Division could still reach remote areas by pickup truck and ATV, but by 2010, because of the IED threat and top-down force-protection requirements, conventional units could barely get to those places at all and had to rely on special operations forces for offensive missions. That overextension meant follow-on units could not sustain the reach earlier units had.

points.h: Two ODA teams: restraint versus aggression
points.body: In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, used an ‘ink spot’ approach, trying to build secure zones around district centers, and refused to enter the Korengal Valley because they recognized something there was baiting them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to get into the Korengal looking for a fight, got entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, was used as muscle by one faction, and started the Korengal ‘snowball’ that escalated into years of intense combat.

points.h: Three US tribes inside the wire could not coexist
points.body: In eastern Afghanistan there were three ‘tribes’ within the US military: conventional forces; the Green Berets, who worked with local partners such as training Afghan National Army commandos and local police; and the joint special operations task force, such as Task Force 373, made up largely of SEAL Team 6 and Rangers, running night raids. The three had different objectives and sometimes supported each other, but more often got in each other's way. The task force might kill someone conventional forces could have easily arrested, while in remote areas conventional forces could not reach, only the task force could operate. That incoherence was a core problem of the Afghanistan war.

points.h: Commanders measured success with the wrong metrics
points.body: Many commanders lacked real understanding of counterinsurgency and could only lean on quantifiable performance metrics: ordnance dropped, miles of road built, number of meetings held. The book gives an example: 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment spent 15 months fighting in Kunar Province and lost 24 soldiers, while its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent, and 10,000 Beanie Babies handed out — metrics that could not reflect actual effects and were sometimes self-contradictory.

Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior US Navy and Air Force generals and admirals have a chapter in their careers that looks nothing like the standard path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams in Kunar and Nuristan provinces in Afghanistan, including submarine officers, nuclear engineers and naval aviators. For example, current INDOPACOM commander Sam Paparo led the PRT in Nuristan for a year. Those assignments overlapped with the fighting at Wana and Narisan, and they rode out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. The experience became a distinctive mark on their careers.

points.h: The military-press relationship went from transparent to hostile
points.body: Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could more or less freely choose which units to embed with, and public affairs just helped him reach company- and platoon-level units. Today, after the embed system effectively ended in 2013-2014, the relationship between the military and the press has deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of officers at battalion level and below sees the media as something terrifying. He argues the turning point was not the McChrystal affair but the second Obama term, when the military began restricting embeds and pushing the war out of sight, because the complicated message that ‘advisors’ were really ‘combat advisors’ was unwelcome.

points.h: How Multicam became a badge of the elite
points.body: Morgan tells the story of how Multicam spread: it was invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art school graduate, lost the Army's camouflage competition (the Army chose the poorly performing ACU pattern), but Delta Force adopted Multicam privately because ACU performed badly at night. It then spread through special operations and became a badge of the elite. Crucially, Crye hinted to game producers that this was elite camouflage, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before it appeared in real photographs, building an elite image in the minds of young soldiers.
